citation: StataCorp, Stata Base Reference Manual, [R] ologit, Example 1, p. 4 (https://www.stata.com/manuals/rologit.pdf; release 19). The page prints the whole dataset as the cross-tabulation `tabulate rep77 foreign`: rep77 Poor 2 domestic and 1 foreign, Fair 10 and 1, Average 20 and 7, Good 13 and 7, Excellent 0 and 5, totalling 45 domestic, 21 foreign and 66 cars. The repair records are the 1977 wave of the 1978 Automobile Data described in [U] 1.2.2 Example datasets.
notes:
THE ROW MARGIN OF THE PUBLISHED CROSS-TABULATION, EXPANDED TO ONE ROW PER CAR, in the order the table reads: rep77 = 1 first, its 2 domestic cars then its 1 foreign one, then rep77 = 2, and so on to rep77 = 5. The manual's own coding is kept -- 1 Poor, 2 Fair, 3 Average, 4 Good, 5 Excellent -- so a cut point reported here can be read against the /cut1 .. /cut4 the page prints. The companion dataset stata_r_ologit_1977_foreign carries the other margin, row for row, and the two share this index, so a case reaching for one must reach for the other.

THE NUMBERS ARE ORDINAL CODES AND NOTHING ELSE, WHICH IS WHY THE MOVE CONTROL BITES ON THE COMPANION AND NOT ON THIS FILE. An ordered model reads only the ORDER of these values, so adding one to every code -- which is what the control's integer move does -- returns the identical fit. The manual says the same thing in its own technical note on the same example: replacing 5 by 10 leaves the estimates unchanged. The companion is an indicator, the control negates it, and every estimate moves with it.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SUPPORT. The cross-tabulation is the WHOLE of the published data for this example, so no other variable of the automobile dataset is here: the manual's Example 2 fits rep77 on foreign, length and mpg, and neither length nor mpg is printed anywhere on the page. Nothing here identifies an individual car, and the order within a cell is this transcription's, not the source's.
